Introduction to fastDiversity

Source: vignettes/fastDiversity-intro.Rmd
fastDiversity-intro.Rmd

Overview

fastDiversity provides fast and flexible calculation of standard population genetic diversity statistics from biallelic SNP data. It is designed for datasets where samples span multiple populations, sites, or species that need to be analysed simultaneously, a common scenario in conservation genomics and comparative population studies.

The package accepts genotype data in standard biallelic dosage format: 0 (homozygous reference, aa), 1 (heterozygous, aA), and 2 (homozygous alternate, AA), with missing data as NA. This format is the output produced by most SNP-calling pipelines.

Installation 

remotes::install_github("eilishmcmaster/fastDiversity")
library(fastDiversity)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggthemes)

Example dataset: Doryphora sassafras

The package ships with SNP data from Doryphora sassafras (Sassafras, Atherospermataceae), a rainforest tree endemic to the eastern Australian coast. The dataset spans five genetic populations, each sampled across multiple sites. This structure, multiple hierarchical grouping levels within a single species, is the typical use case for fastDiversity.

data(example_data)

# Genotype matrix: rows are samples, columns are SNP loci
# Values are 0 (aa), 1 (aA), 2 (AA), or NA (missing)
dim(example_gt)
#> [1]  257 1906

example_print <- example_gt[c(1,100,150,200,250), 1:10]
colnames(example_print) <- NULL
example_print
#>                               
#> NSW1008199 0 2 0 2 0 0 1 1 1 1
#> NSW1015673 0 1 1 2 2 0 2 1 1 0
#> NSW1014534 2 0 1 1 2 1 0 0 1 0
#> NSW1088929 2 0 2 1 2 1 1 0 0 1
#> NSW1146190 2 0 1 1 2 1 0 1 0 0
# Metadata: one row per sample, matching the row order of example_gt
head(example_meta)

#> 1 NSW1008199 Wambam_Creek          5
#> 2 NSW1008169 Wambam_Creek          5

The row order of example_gt must match the row order of example_meta, the nth row of the genotype matrix corresponds to the nth row of the metadata.

Principal coordinates analysis

A distance-based PCA provides an intuitive overview of genetic structure across individuals. PC scores are computed from pairwise genetic distances and merged with metadata for plotting:

pca   <- prcomp(dist(example_gt), center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
s_pca <- summary(pca)

# Axis labels showing % variance explained
importance <- s_pca[["importance"]][2, ]
axis_names  <- paste0(names(importance), " (", round(importance * 100, 1), "%)")

# Merge PC scores with sample metadata
pcs <- pca$x %>%
  data.frame() %>%
  merge(example_meta, by.x = 0, by.y = "sample")

ggplot(pcs, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = factor(population))) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title  = expression("PCA of SNP genotypes"),
    x      = axis_names[1],
    y      = axis_names[2],
    color  = "Population"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

Clustering of samples in PCA space corroborates the population structure indicated by the diversity statistics and private allele analysis.

Allele sharing and private alleles

Understanding which alleles are unique to a single population (private) versus shared across populations is a useful first step in assessing population distinctiveness. Populations with many private alleles may represent distinct evolutionary lineages that warrant separate management.

Step 1: Build the allele list

make_allele_list() takes the genotype matrix and a grouping vector and returns a named list of allele sets, one per group.

allele_list_population <- make_allele_list(example_gt, example_meta$population)
#> There are  57  samples in  5 
#> There are  31  samples in  4 
#> There are  46  samples in  3 
#> There are  23  samples in  2 
#> There are  100  samples in  1

names(allele_list_population)
#> [1] "5" "4" "3" "2" "1"

Step 2: Visualise allele overlap

Because the result is a standard named list, it works directly with ggvenn:

ggvenn::ggvenn(allele_list_population, 
               stroke_size=0)+
  ggtitle("Allele sharing among populations")

Alternatively, an upset plot may be easier to read:

ggVennDiagram::plot_upset(ggVennDiagram::Venn(allele_list_population), sets.bar.show.numbers = FALSE)

This shows how much allelic diversity is shared across populations versus restricted to individual groups. A large exclusive region indicates a genetically distinct population.

Step 3: Count private and total alleles 

private_total_alleles_population <- calculate_private_alleles(allele_list_population)

private_total_alleles_population
#>   population private_allele_count total_allele_count
#> 1          5                   16               3475
#> 2          4                    1               3515
#> 3          3                    0               3372
#> 4          2                    0               3178
#> 5          1                   54               3471
#> 6      Total                 3812               3812

The output gives private allele counts (alleles found in only one population) and total allele counts per group. These can be used directly in reporting or joined to the main statistics table (shown below).

Diversity statistics with faststats()

faststats() calculates allelic richness, heterozygosity, inbreeding coefficients, and population differentiation for each combination of genetic group and site, with locus-level filtering applied independently within each genetic group.

Filtering parameters

Parameter Description
minimum_n Exclude sites with fewer than this many individuals
minimum_loci Exclude genetic groups where fewer than this many loci pass filtering
maf Minor allele frequency threshold: loci below this value are excluded per genetic group (typically 0.05)
max_missingness Exclude loci missing in more than this proportion of samples within a group (e.g. 0.3 removes loci missing in >30% of samples)

Filtering is applied within each genetic group independently. A locus retained for one population may be excluded for another if it fails MAF or missingness thresholds in that group, an important distinction from global pre-filtering, which can retain uninformative loci in some groups or discard informative ones in others.

Running faststats

genetic_group_variable defines the level at which locus filtering is applied (e.g. species or population). site_variable defines the grouping unit for which statistics are calculated (e.g. sampling site). The function returns one row per unique genetic group × site combination.

basicstats <- faststats(
  gt                    = example_gt,
  genetic_group_variable = example_meta$population,
  site_variable         = example_meta$site,
  minimum_n             = 6,
  minimum_loci          = 50,
  maf                   = 0.05,
  max_missingness       = 0.3
)
#> [1] "1 complete"
#> [1] "2 complete"
#> [1] "3 complete"
#> [1] "4 complete"
#> [1] "5 complete"
#> [1] "Process complete!"

head(basicstats)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 11
#>   group site               Ar    Ho    He    uHe   Fis   Fst   uFis  loci  n    
#>   <chr> <chr>              <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>
#> 1 1     Airdrop_Rd         1.25… 0.26… 0.25… 0.283 -0.0… 0.14… 0.05… 844   6    
#> 2 1     Big_Scrub Loop1    1.28… 0.28… 0.26… 0.28… -0.1… 0.12… -0.0… 844   6    
#> 3 1     Big_Scrub Loop2    1.25… 0.26… 0.26… 0.29… 0.02… 0.09… 0.11… 844   6    
#> 4 1     Binna_Burra        1.25… 0.26… 0.25… 0.27… -0.0… 0.15… 0.05… 844   6    
#> 5 1     Gibbergunyah Nigh… 1.25… 0.25… 0.28… 0.29… 0.09… 0.05… 0.14… 844   11   
#> 6 1     Koonyum_Range      1.22… 0.23… 0.21… 0.24… -0.0… 0.26… 0.04… 844   6

Output columns explained

Column Description
group Genetic group ID (e.g. population, species)
site Site ID
Ar Allelic richness per site per group, standardised for sample size
Ho Observed heterozygosity: proportion of heterozygous loci averaged across individuals
He Expected heterozygosity under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium within site_variable
uHe Unbiased expected heterozygosity (corrected for small sample size)
Fis Inbreeding coefficient (1 - Ho/He). Positive values indicate excess homozygosity; negative values indicate excess heterozygosity
uFis Unbiased inbreeding coefficient (1 - Ho/uHe)
Fst Population differentiation: Weir & Cockerham (1984) FST, calculated as (Ht - Hs) / Ht
loci Number of loci retained after filtering for this group
n Number of individuals sampled at this site x group combination

Plotting diversity statistics

Because faststats() returns one row per site, each population contributes multiple points, one per site. A faceted multi-panel plot gives a simultaneous overview of heterozygosity, inbreeding, and differentiation:

library(tidyr)

stats_long <- basicstats %>%
  mutate(across(c(Ho, He, Fis, Fst), as.numeric)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(Ho, He, Fis, Fst),
    names_to  = "statistic",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(statistic = factor(statistic,
    levels = c("Ho", "He", "Fis", "Fst"),
    labels = c("Observed heterozygosity (Ho)",
               "Expected heterozygosity (He)",
               "Inbreeding coefficient (Fis)",
               "Fixation index (Fst)")
  ))

ggplot(stats_long, aes(x = group, y = value, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.6, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 1.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Diversity statistics",
    x     = "Population",
    y     = NULL
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position  = "none",
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey92"),
    strip.text       = element_text(size = 9)
  )

Optional: bootstrapped confidence intervals

For published reporting, bootstrapped confidence intervals can be added around Ho, He, and Fis. Two resampling strategies are available:

  • By loci (get_CI_loci_resampling = TRUE): analogous to hierfstat::boot.ppfis : loci are resampled with replacement to quantify how sensitive statistics are to the choice of markers.
  • By individuals (get_CI_individual_resampling = TRUE): analogous to diveRsity::basicstats : individuals are resampled with replacement to quantify sampling uncertainty.
basicstats_ci <- faststats(
  gt                     = example_gt,
  genetic_group_variable = example_meta$population,
  site_variable          = example_meta$site,
  minimum_n              = 6,
  minimum_loci           = 50,
  maf                    = 0.05,
  max_missingness        = 0.3,
  get_CI_loci_resampling = TRUE,
  boots                  = 100,
  CI_alpha               = 0.05
)

CI columns are appended with a prefix for the resampling strategy (loci_ or ind_) and a suffix for the statistic and quantile boundary (e.g. loci_ho.2.5%, loci_ho.97.5%). These plug directly into geom_pointrange():

ggplot(basicstats_ci, aes(x = group, y = as.numeric(Ho), colour = group)) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(
      ymin = as.numeric(`loci_ho.2.5%`),
      ymax = as.numeric(`loci_ho.97.5%`)
    ),
    position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, seed = 1),
    size = 0.6
  ) +
  labs(
    title = expression("Ho ± 95% CI (loci bootstrap)"),
    x = "Population",
    y = "Observed heterozygosity (Ho)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Optional: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium testing

faststats() can test whether allele frequencies at each site deviate significantly from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium expectations using Fisher’s exact test, with p-values combined across loci using Fisher’s method:

basicstats_hwe <- suppressWarnings( faststats(
  gt                     = example_gt,
  genetic_group_variable = example_meta$population,
  site_variable          = example_meta$population,
  minimum_n              = 6,
  minimum_loci           = 50,
  maf                    = 0.05,
  max_missingness        = 0.3,
  run_HWE_test           = TRUE,
  return_locus_stats     = FALSE   # set TRUE to retrieve per-locus p-values
))

basicstats_hwe[,c("site", "Ho", "He", "Fis", "Fst", "loci", "n", "HWE_p")]

The HW_fisher_p column gives the combined p-value per site. Sites with values below the chosen alpha threshold show significant deviation from HWE, which may reflect inbreeding, cryptic population structure within a site, selection at linked loci, or genotyping artefacts.

Individual-level statistics

In addition to site-level summaries, fastDiversity provides two functions for calculating statistics at the level of individual samples. These are useful for examining variation in inbreeding and heterozygosity on an individual basis, which can be informative for fitness and hybridisation.

Both functions apply the same locus-level filtering as faststats(): MAF and missingness thresholds are applied per genetic group before calculation, ensuring that individual estimates are based on the same high-quality, informative loci used in population-level analyses.

Individual multilocus heterozygosity

individual_Ho() calculates multilocus heterozygosity (MLH) for each sample: the proportion of retained loci that are heterozygous in that individual.

ind_MLH_ho <- individual_Ho(
  example_gt,
  genetic_group_variable = example_meta$population,
  maf                    = 0.05,
  max_missingness        = 0.3
)

head(ind_MLH_ho)
#> NSW1008199 NSW1008169 NSW1008189 NSW1008229 NSW1008224 NSW1009574 
#>  0.3719705  0.2673913  0.2556880  0.2719298  0.2706522  0.3679834

Individual inbreeding coefficient (Wright’s F)

individual_F() calculates Wright’s inbreeding coefficient for each sample: F = 1 − (Ho / He), where He is calculated across the genetic group. This measures the probability that both alleles at a locus are identical by descent (Frankham, Ballou & Briscoe 2010). Because He is calculated at the group level rather than across genetic groups, estimates are not deflated by the Wahlund effect that would arise from pooling genetically differentiated individuals.

ind_F <- individual_F(
  example_gt,
  genetic_group_variable = example_meta$population,
  maf                    = 0.05,
  max_missingness        = 0.3
)

head(ind_F)
#> NSW1008199 NSW1008169 NSW1008189 NSW1008229 NSW1008224 NSW1009574 
#> 0.01264873 0.29024170 0.32130680 0.27819474 0.28158612 0.02323208

Relating MLH to F

Plotting individual MLH against F reveals the expected negative relationship: individuals with higher observed heterozygosity have lower inbreeding coefficients.

# Combine into a data frame and add population labels
ind_df <- data.frame(
  sample     = names(ind_MLH_ho),
  MLH        = as.numeric(ind_MLH_ho),
  F          = as.numeric(ind_F)
) %>%
  merge(example_meta, by = "sample")

ggplot(ind_df, aes(x = MLH, y = F, colour = as.factor(population))) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(
    title    = expression("Individual MLH vs inbreeding coefficient"),
    x        = "Multilocus heterozygosity (Ho)",
    y        = expression(paste("Inbreeding coefficient (", italic(F), ")")),
    colour   = "Population"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

Nucleotide diversity and Tajima’s D

pi_theta_d_stats() calculates nucleotide diversity (pi), Wu & Watterson’s theta (W), the number of segregating sites (S), and Tajima’s D for each genetic site_variable specified within genetic_group_variable. The implementation follows the missing-data-aware approach of Korunes & Samuk (2021), meaning that loci with missing genotypes contribute proportionally rather than being excluded entirely, an important correction for RADseq and DArTseq data where missingness is common.

Running pi_theta_d_stats

When n = NULL, all individuals at each site are used. The n argument can be set to a fixed integer to subsample individuals, which allows comparison across sites with unequal sample sizes:

# Use all available individuals per population
D_n_all <- pi_theta_d_stats(
  example_gt,
  genetic_group_variable = example_meta$population,
  site_variable          = example_meta$population,
  n                      = NULL,
  minimum_n              = 5,
  minimum_loci           = 5,
  max_missingness        = 0.1,
  maf                    = 0,
  allele_count_min       = 0
)
#> [1] "Process complete!"

# Subsample to 20 individuals per population
D_n_20 <- pi_theta_d_stats(
  example_gt,
  genetic_group_variable = example_meta$population,
  site_variable          = example_meta$population,
  n                      = 20,
  minimum_n              = 5,
  minimum_loci           = 5,
  max_missingness        = 0.1,
  maf                    = 0,
  allele_count_min       = 0
)
#> [1] "Process complete!"

# Subsample to 10 individuals per population
D_n_10 <- pi_theta_d_stats(
  example_gt,
  genetic_group_variable = example_meta$population,
  site_variable          = example_meta$population,
  n                      = 10,
  minimum_n              = 5,
  minimum_loci           = 5,
  max_missingness        = 0.1,
  maf                    = 0,
  allele_count_min       = 0
)
#> [1] "Process complete!"

# Subsample to 5 individuals per population
D_n_5 <- pi_theta_d_stats(
  example_gt,
  genetic_group_variable = example_meta$population,
  site_variable          = example_meta$population,
  n                      = 5,
  minimum_n              = 5,
  minimum_loci           = 5,
  max_missingness        = 0.1,
  maf                    = 0,
  allele_count_min       = 0
)
#> [1] "Process complete!"

Output columns explained

Column Description
group Genetic group ID
site Site ID
loci Number of loci retained after filtering
n Number of individuals used
pi Nucleotide diversity: mean pairwise differences across loci
S Number of segregating (polymorphic) sites
theta Wu & Watterson’s theta: diversity estimate based on S, corrected for sample size
D Tajima’s D: standardised difference between pi and W. Negative values suggest an excess of rare variants (population expansion or purifying selection); positive values suggest an excess of intermediate-frequency variants (balancing selection or population contraction)
real_missingness Proportion of missing data in the filtered matrix used for calculation

Effect of sample size on diversity estimates

A key feature of pi_theta_d_stats() is the n argument, which subsamples individuals to a fixed number before calculation. This allows fair comparison across populations with unequal sample sizes. However, sample size affects estimates differently: S is particularly sensitive to n because larger samples are more likely to capture rare variants, which inflates W relative to pi and therefore pulls D negative.

The plot below illustrates this by comparing estimates across three levels of subsampling:

library(tidyr)

# Combine results and label by sample size used
D_combined <- bind_rows(
  D_n_all %>% mutate(sample_size = paste0("All (n=", n, ")")),
  D_n_20  %>% mutate(sample_size = "n = 20"),
  D_n_10  %>% mutate(sample_size = "n = 10"),
  D_n_5   %>% mutate(sample_size = "n = 5")
) %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(pi, S, theta, D), as.numeric),
    sample_size = factor(sample_size,
                         levels = c("n = 5", "n = 10", "n = 20",
                                    unique(D_n_all %>%
                                             mutate(l = paste0("All (n=", n, ")")) %>%
                                             pull(l))))
  )

# Reshape to long for faceting
D_long <- D_combined %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(pi, S, theta, D),
               names_to  = "statistic",
               values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(statistic = factor(statistic,
    levels = c("pi", "theta", "S", "D"),
    labels = c("Nucleotide diversity (pi)",
               "Wu & Watterson's theta (W)",
               "Segregating sites (S)",
               "Tajima's D")))

ggplot(D_long, aes(x = group, y = value, colour = sample_size,
                   group = sample_size)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ statistic, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title   = expression("Effect of sample size on diversity statistics"),
    x       = "Population",
    y       = NULL,
    colour  = "Sample size"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey92"),
    strip.text       = element_text(size = 9),
    legend.position  = "bottom"
  )
